Hi Hannah,

Thanks for the demo last week — team was really impressed with the latency profiles. Date: Fri, 2 Oct 2026 10:20:00 -0700
Subject: INTERNAL: TempestAI sizing ask — need validation

Team — quick internal thread. Tempest provided samples and wants a committed recommendation that meets p95 <= 250ms for generation. Key inputs:
- steady-state: ~1.2M tokens/day (~14 tokens/sec averaged over 24h) but business hours concentration means higher TPS during peaks
- typical request length: 120 tokens (median), tails up to 400 tokens
- peak bursts: 20 TPS normal, 200 TPS spikes (2–3m)

Attached is my initial workbook (tempest_commit_plan_v1.xlsx) with two candidate slabs:
A) 4 x A100-equivalent GPUs (continuous throughput estimate: ~180 TPS for model family X-3b quantized) + 20% burst headroom
B) 6 x A100-equivalent GPUs (continuous throughput estimate: ~270 TPS for same topology) + 40% headroom + dedicated burst pool for 3–5 minute surges

Questions for Ben / Jonas: are kernel-level throughput estimates realistic given frequent 120-token requests and KV-cache hit ~70%? What would you recommend for scheduled warmup and cache prefill to avoid p95 spikes at start of business hours?

Thanks — Hannah

From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>

Date: Fri, 2 Oct 2026 14:40:12 -0700
Subject: Re: INTERNAL: TempestAI sizing ask — need validation

Hannah — did a quick run using Tempest's sample and our perf matrix for the X-3b family (quantized fp16 path). Notes: 
- Measured sustained tokens/sec per A100-equivalent for median 120-token requests with 70% KV hit ~= 45 tokens/sec/GPU. That implies ~4 GPUs for sustained ~180 TPS (matches your calc A).
- For p95 <= 250ms: if model is multi-turn and context hits are high, the p95 is dominated by kernel latency and NVLink shuffles. Our empirical p95 at 180 TPS was ~230ms (with optimized kernel path and prewarmed KV caches).
- 200 TPS spikes for 2–3 minutes: running pure 4-GPU slab will saturate. We recommend one of the following: add a 1–2 GPU burst pool (hot spare) OR accept a degraded p95 (up to ~350 ms) during those short spikes.

Recommended commercial options: 
Option 1 (lower TCO): Commit to 4-GPU slab + add dynamic burst credit allowing routing to shared burst pool (best-effort). Expect occasional p95 bump during 200 TPS spikes.
Option 2 (SLA-sensitive): Commit 6-GPU slab with reserved burst cushion to keep p95 < 250ms during 200 TPS spikes; ~+50% monthly cost.

Operational notes:
- Warmup: schedule a 10–15 minute cache prefill 15 minutes before business hours using a synthetic request set (we can provide script).
- Autoscale: we can configure a short-duration autoscale policy for 3–5 minute spikes if customer opts into dedicated burst GPUs.

I’ve attached a short note (redwood_sizing_notes.pdf) with the throughput math and tested p95 curves.

—Ben
Solutions Engineering, Redwood Inference

Attachments: redwood_sizing_notes.pdf

Liam

Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity question + sample usage — follow ups

Liam — quick answers and a concrete next step: 
1) Option 1 spike risk: based on our historical workload simulations the probability that a 2–3 minute 200 TPS spike causes p95 > 250ms is ~65% if routed to a 4-GPU slab without burst pool. If you enable shared burst credits (best-effort routing) we estimate the p95 breach reduces to ~30% because some requests will spill to other pools.
2) Ballpark monthly delta: Option 1 (4-GPU slab + shared burst credits) ~ $28k/mo. Option 2 (6-GPU slab reserved) ~ $42k/mo. Exact numbers will be in the commercial sheet but those are the ranges for execs.
3) Warmup: we can provide the warmup script and run a validation test within 48 business hours in our staging environment once we receive a signed NDA / access token. We’ll also do a 1-hr soak to validate p95 curves.

Next step: if you’re okay with the executive numbers I’ll share a formal commercial (quarterly commit option + 20% burst buffer) and schedule a follow-up call with Ben and Jonas to walk ops through warmup and autoscale behaviors.

Thanks — Hannah
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference
